title.narrative: NIHR HPSR-CA - Harmful alcohol use in Southern Africa: studying drivers of drinking for effective intervention

description.narrative:
Harmful alcohol use is a substantial problem globally with negative impacts on health and wellbeing. The alcohol industry is a key driver of consumption or harms. It has responded to reduced consumption in many high-income countries (from increased regulation) by developing new sources of growth or profit in lower- and middle-income countries (LMICs) where harms are greater and policies are weaker. Expansion into Africa, with South Africa (SA) as a gateway, is an explicit part of this strategy. Many factors influence how much people drink, which vary from country to country: how easy or affordable is it to purchase alcohol, prevailing attitudes or ideas about drinking, and where or what type of alcohol people usually drink. It is usually the country’s alcohol policy (i.e. regulations about when/where alcohol can be sold) and enforcement that determine these factors.
A research collaboration comprising the University of Cape Town, the South African Medical Research Council, Centre for the AIDS Programme of Research in South Africa, the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine (LSHTM) and the University of Botswana will conduct the research in South Africa and Botswana from January 2025 to December 2029, focused on three sites in each of two provinces in South Africa (Khayelitsha, Klipfontein and Klapmuts in the Western Cape, and Atteridgeville, Olievenhoutbosch and Ga-Rankuwa in Gauteng) and three study sites in Botswana (Gaborone, Tlokweng and Francistown).
We will review, consolidate, and synthesise existing literature on the influence of political, economic, and regulatory contexts on local alcohol environments, iteratively map alcohol supply chains through documentary review and stakeholder engagement, and conduct a desk-based review of national and selected provincial and local laws, regulations and policies. In each study site, we will also map and describe alcohol outlets, conduct interviews and focus groups with vendors, alcohol consumers and non-drinking community members, and in each South African study site household surveys to understand the relationship between drinking patterns/behaviour and health/social outcomes. We will apply modelled provincial alcohol harm estimates to derive harm reduction scenarios, provide consolidated and accessible evidence for communities/policymakers to inform potential prevention interventions and document the data requirements for effectively monitoring the alcohol environment.

This project has 5 objectives:
1. Examine business and political strategies that the alcohol industry uses to influence policy and regulation at a global level before considering how these strategies are applied locally. 2. Describe the context in which people in South Africa and Botswana buy and consume alcohol and how these impact drinking patterns and behaviour. This will include mapping and visiting alcohol outlets, observing behaviour when buying/drinking, and interviewing people who sell and drink alcohol and those who do not. 3. Investigate how drinking patterns and behaviour impact health using existing data and data we collect in our study sites. By using mathematical models, we will explore the possible impact of proposed interventions and policy changes on alcohol-related harm, as well as consumption or sales in South Africa. 4. Harness community voices to influence alcohol policy by using research outputs that we co-create with community and policy stakeholders in South Africa and Botswana. 5. Strengthen capacity for both research through formal training (PhD and Master's students) and skills transfer, and through community engagement and involvement at the organisational and network levels.
